utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Ivetic, if you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to begin first with some corrections to the record from yesterday and to address the one request that you had asked us to look into. At transcript page 44723, lines 7 through 14, we were asked to clarify a reference to paragraph 34 of the Prosecution final brief. The reference was actually to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, paragraph 34, where the statement: "Creating parallel Serb civilian and military structures" was quoted from. At transcript page 44730, line 11, the reference to P324 was actually meant to be a reference to P3029, page 324. At transcript page 44732, lines 22 to 24, in answer to Your Honour's question, the date of the Exhibit D193 is January 20th, 1993. And at T44735, line 22, the reference to P3906 should refer to P3806. And those are the corrections and responses that I had for Your Honours. And now I'd like to start by talking about Sarajevo. The Prosecution the other day started talking about G1 as a massive bombardment in Sarajevo and the many casualties that resulted therefrom, choosing to go highlight the only victim witness they brought, Ms. Fadila Tarcin. I find it insulting to Ms. Tarcin and to the Defence that Mr. Weber callously used a 16-year-old girl to highlight the alleged lack of legitimate military targets in Sirokaca but failed to mention that the mortar shell which destroyed her life and limits her mobility came from Alija Izetbegovic's Sarajevo forces, not the Bosnian Serb side, as she testified at transcript page 3447 to 3448 when we said the shell came from the city, not from up the hill where the Serbs were. The Prosecution acts sometimes as if they are covering up the crimes of Alija Izetbegovic's forces rather than as a Prosecutor. Similarly, for unscheduled Vase Miskina, they hide from sight any mention of Ambassador Cutileiro's testimony that the Portuguese UN artillery officer performing the investigation likewise said that Izetbegovic's forces, the ABiH, were to blame there as well. That was at transcript page -- I think I have a wrong reference. It was in the statement of Mr. Cutileiro and when he testified in court in these proceedings. Like all wars, the conflict in Sarajevo started long before the first shot was ever fired. As you well know, it was born of the nationalist fervor rampant throughout Bosnia at that time and the increasingly more pervasive efforts of Izetbegovic to secure political dominance for himself and the SDA at the expense of the other constituent peoples of Bosnia. In the words of Witness Kecmanovic about the vote for independence: "It wasn't just about the event but the importance was that ethnic equality was violated." Transcript page 23813. When it became clear that Izetbegovic was not going to be available to achieve his goals through democratic, political means, he began to enact a plan to secure these objectives by force, saying: "I am prepared to sacrifice peace for Bosnia-Herzegovina." We find that at D735, paragraph 45. In pursuit of this, the SDA illegally imported and distributed weapons throughout Sarajevo, trained paramilitary groups, stacked government departments, including the MUP, and set up secret groups, like the Seve. This is discussed at paragraphs 1683 to 1710 of our final brief. The SDA promoted discord within the community; and, as the number of unpunished attacks against Bosnian Serbs rose, so too did the real fear that the Bosnian Serbs as a peoples would be subjugated by the SDA. As the prospect of war became an imminent reality, the SDA scrambled to establish an organised defence in Sarajevo. Formed officially on 22 May 1992 which is after the establishment of the ABiH - we see that in D270 read together with P2008 - it took in reality some time before the SRK, if ever, constituted a unified corps. The ABiH were stronger in number, were better armed and possessed superior weaponry, D468; transcript page 25846; D482; D658. The ABiH took control of Sarajevo. Using mobile mortars mounted on the back of vehicles, they showed themselves as a highly mobile force. Witness Vujasin talked about that at D641. The ABiH maintained their weaponry and ammunition stocks by illegally smuggling them in through humanitarian aid convoys and later the tunnel under the airport. The ABiH used the presence of civilians in the city to protect themselves, hiding their command posts in local shops and post offices, establishing weapons facilities in residential buildings and basements, training new recruits in primary schools alongside children sitting their daily lessons, positioning their snipers in high-rise towers and so on. You could see some of that at paragraph 1765 of the Defence brief. Witness Draskovic, a member of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade in Novo Sarajevo testified at page 38044 as follows: "... there was sniping around the clock ... one could not be certain at any point during the 24 hours, for example, even our guards were not safe in their posts, although they had fortifications, but there was always some opportunity for the sharpshooters having night-vision, hence we were exposed to their fire round-the-clock and we were unable to move. That very fact, that one is just waiting for your wrong step at any point in time that can end your life, makes you feel very uncomfortable and that is how this terror occurred on the side of our soldiers and civilians." It is an absurd proposition to suggest that the SRK and the people of Republika Srpska should have given over their ethnic equality without complaint, should have submitted to the unlawful attacks of the ABiH at the commencement of the conflict, and thereafter should have allowed illegal smuggling to continue unabated, should have merely submitted to the incessant sniping and shelling that ensued from the ABiH side, should have silently counted up their dead and injured. That is, however, what the international community demanded of them. Indeed, the SRK was repeatedly forbidden by General Mladic to fire unless absolutely necessary to do so. This applied particularly during cease-fires, which it should be noted, General Mladic consistently sought in order to give the politicians the opportunity to find a peaceful solution to the dispute. We see that at D66, P5031, D150, D1575, D1707, among others. Izetbegovic, however, had little regard for cease-fires or peace agreements, as seen in D1426. He wanted war and the political gain that war would bring him. He wanted it so adamantly he is reported to have said he would "... only accept intervention or death for his people as final solution." That's from D1426, page 1. Izetbegovic and the BiH leadership did all they could, therefore, to perpetuate the crisis and to portray themselves as the victims of indiscriminate aggressions. "The shelling has reduced considerably in Sarajevo" wrote the UNPROFOR Sarajevo on page 2 of D1426, "but the Presidency continues to perpetuate the myth that the city is being bombarded. This is not the case, however; it is the version of a man who expects international military help." It was the worst-kept secret in Sarajevo, that the need of the BiH to perpetuate this narrative was of such importance to them that they shelled and sniped at their own people. Indeed, General Rose admitted that he knew Ganic organised his secret police to snipe at trams and to do so at an angle that matched the Serb line so that the SRK would be blamed, T8736 to 8737. A point confirmed by the confession of Hereneda, a prominent member of Seve who sniped at civilians and UN personnel in just such a manner at Witness Garaplija testified about, transcript page 33909. Skrba, a company commander in the 1st Smbr, recalled that massacres that were committed by the ABiH 10th Mountain Brigade against civilians in their zone of responsibility, D524, paragraph 7. Witness Dragicevic recalled the frequent ABiH fire upon schools kindergartens, hospitals, and apartment blocks, at D554, paragraph 29. And Grey, an UNMO, testified that the ABiH self-targeting was particularly prominent during visits of international personnel, when media were present, or the BiH wanted to get Sarajevo "back on the front page." D116, paragraph 3; and see paragraphs 1861 to 1867 of the Defence final brief. RM413, for example, noted that: "... on several occasions that in spots which were particularly accessible to the media, sniping occurred that could only have come from within the city itself." P640, page 4. By hiding in amongst civilian features, using civilians as shields in deliberate contravention of Article 51 of the AP I of the Geneva Conventions and firing upon their own people, Izetbegovic and the ABiH brought the war to the very door-step of those who least desired it. Not coincidentally, the ABiH was particularly concerned to hide their activities and even expelled OPS Officer Captain Hansen, assistant to UNMO Per Oien, in June 1995 when he told the BiH liaison officer to stop firing on their own people after witnessing an ABiH attack on the PTT [sic] building. We have that from Witness Oien at transcript page 43192 through 43195. This expulsion was misrepresented by the Prosecution in their closing arguments last week. At transcript page 44516, Mr. Weber focuses on how the Defence is trying to use "supposed events" without any inspiring basis as to this "alleged" firing of the ABiH on their own PTT building involving UNMO Hansen. Your Honours, I feel compelled to point out that what Mr. Weber sees as "defence" and "supposed events" without basis comes from a Prosecution witness statement taken by Mr. Weber's office from Mr. Hansen, where Prosecution counsel - and not the Defence - collected the very information relied upon by the Defence. Mr. Weber would have us ignore the very telling part of the same which was presented in court in this case which says: "In that period, there were a lot of homemade airplane bombs that landed in that area; it has to be about ten in the two weeks before the hit on the TV building. On observation post could see that some of the bombs were fired from Ilidza on the BSA side. I was informed by an UNMO who had seen the shelling on the TV building that this particular bomb that had impacted on the TV building was fired from the BiH side. Another UNMO who heard the bomb told me that the bomb only flew for a short period, so that fitted with the findings of the first UNMO that the bomb was fired from BiH-hold territory. I sent my report about this event to my superiors by secure means."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, we usually receive references to exhibit numbers. Is there any reason why we have 65 ter numbers here rather than exhibit numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is a witness statement taken for purposes of litigation, and therefore it cannot be introduced into evidence under Rule 92 without the witness appearing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's not in evidence, then I think we should not be --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this part that I read out was read out in court and presented to a witness, and we have testimony of Mr. Jan Segers and Mr. Per Oien in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would except you to quote from the transcript rather than to more or less invite us to look into documents which are not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I did quote from the transcript because in that transcript I read from this document, as I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if you now give us the transcript references which make it is easier for us to find the source of what you are saying in the evidence as admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Transcript page 43812 through 3, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And we can remove this from our screens as not being in evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Similarly, Jan Segers - another UN witness - confirmed that he knew of another instance where the same thing happened and the complaining UNMO was kicked out by the ABiH. So I therefore reject Mr. Weber's comments that this was somehow made up by the Defence and inserted into a Prosecution's witness statement. That they would stoop to such cheap tactics only shows their desire to win the case at all cost, even at the cost of their own department's integrity. Your Honours, I will shift tack now to discuss the Prosecution's assertions that the engagement of targets in Sarajevo was done in an indiscriminate and disproportionate manner. Prosecution suggest this was evidenced by the targeting of ostensibly civilian targets, the impact of shells at some distance from the line of confrontation, and the so-called bombardments of the city. In fact, the SRK was careful not to engage civilians or civilian targets which had been confirmed as such by visual observations or information gathered from informants and persons who had fled Sarajevo. Transcript page 38460, Witness Tusevljak; D535, paragraph 136; D824; D825; D643, paragraph 41; D540; D468, paragraph 12; and D658, paragraph 14, are some of the evidence talking about that. The list of known ABiH positions was long and reveals the extent to which the ABiH abused civilian features. It included significant ABiH deployment throughout the neighbourhood of Hrasnica, including the four command posts of the 104th Brigade at Hrasnicki Stan, D559, Witness Sehovac, paragraph 21; and the ABiH special forces training centre at the Alekse Santic school, also Witness Sehovac and the same exhibit. It also includes an extensive number of positions in Centar, Stup, and Alipasino Polje including the PTT building, D2015, page 3. Mejtas, Pofalici where the PTT building was located, D1412, Witness Grey, paragraph 9. The many positions in Dolac-Malta including the Unis sky-scraper, D647, page 2. At least five positions in Kosevo, two in Bjelave, including the students' hostel, D647, page 2. And countless others, scattered in particular in old town Bascarsija and across Sokolje, Butmir, Dobrinja, Nedzarici, Otoka, Vojnicko Polje, Cengic Vila, Buca Potok, Soukbunar/Kovacici, to name just a few. It should be noted that this list is not even close to exhaustive and does not include the various military patrols, mobile mortar, and congregations of troops which also occurred throughout Sarajevo. Even the city ambulances were used as taxis by local politicians and for the transport of ammunition rather than for patients. And mobile mortars regularly fired from the grounds of both hospitals, in a base tactic, described by Witness Jordan at transcript page 1819 as "pointless and inaccurate," threatening not only the civilians located outside of Sarajevo but those within, given the tendency of these mobile mortars to "fall short." A phenomenon which occurred more frequently than anybody would like, particularly when the mortar was hastily set up, as Jordan testified at transcript page 1818 to 1819. The very presence of mobile mortars in Sarajevo calls into question the Prosecution's allegation that the SRK fired indiscriminately and is consistent with the findings of the Gotovina's Appeals Chamber which found at paragraph 66 of the Judgement that the presence of mobile mortars: "... raises reasonable doubt whether even artillery impact sites particularly distant from fixed artillery targets considered legitimate... demonstrate that unlawful shelling took place." This finding, in relation to Sarajevo is more pronounced given that the international witnesses were unaware of the vast majority of ABiH positions or the positions of mobile mortars at any time, P421, paragraph 72 and 128; the testimony of Witnesses Fraser and Mole at 5876 to 5877 and 4346 to 4357 of the transcript. This ignorance stemmed - at least in part - from the imbalance on UN observation posts in the territory of each party, the bias system of recording shelling in and around Sarajevo, and the politically aligned agendas of certain international personnel which will be discussed further in due course. Transcript page 4304, Witness Mole; P503, Witness Thomas, paragraph 19, 35, 37; P504, paragraph 2. Given the biases, internationals were not in a position to judge the fire of the SRK as indiscriminate, and this undermines their assertions about both the origin and the impact of artillery, mortar, and small-arms fire in Sarajevo. Indeed, at paragraph 79 of the Gotovina appeals Judgement, it was effectively held that the observations of witnesses - with no artillery experience and whose vantage points made it difficult to determine where the shells were directed at or actually landed - were not sufficient to base a finding that the shelling was indiscriminate. These findings have not, it seems, influenced the Prosecution, who - it seems - has wholeheartedly adopted the assumptions of many internationals with such enthusiasm that they have neglected their duty to evidence the culpability of the SRK for such events, Scheduled incidents G4, F11, F13, and in fact most, if not all, of the F and G incidents. The Prosecution has been so enthusiastic, they've even alleged SRK responsibility for incidents for which the evidence and the international witnesses suggest the SRK weren't responsible; Vase Miskina, for example, and both scheduled Markale incidents, G8 and G18. In G8, for example, the Prosecution dismiss all evidence contrary to their position as being part of some Defence "conspiracy theory." In doing so, they would have you conveniently ignore not only the findings of Defence expert Subotic and numerous UN investigations which could not determine the origin of fire with any degree of certainty, as discussed in paragraph 1996 to 2062 of our final brief. But would also have you ignore the words of Segers who said: "We are almost certain that it was not the Serbs." D1466, page 6. And another UN witness, Russell, who believed that the shell had come from a location closer rather than further from the crater, D1219, paragraph 22. I'd like to go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is much easier for the Prosecution to pretend these are conspiracy theories than to admit what the evidence shows, that SRK culpability for this incident cannot be established beyond a reasonable doubt. A similarly selective narrative has been adopted by the Prosecution for incident G18. There, the Prosecution relies essentially on the report of Colonel Powers, whose conclusions depart from all prior investigations, P797, page 21. The Prosecution has led no evidence to justify this departure nor to explain why his findings should be accepted. They suggest only that the findings were influenced by a meeting between Powers and the Force Commander, and the chief UNMO, a suggestion dismissed by Lieutenant-Colonel Per Oien, who reviewed all reports of the incident and testified there was no chief UNMO, and he did not receive any such report from Powers as is discussed in our final brief at paragraphs 2083 and 2084. Powers, as it turns out, was the American liaison between NATO and General Smith, an UNPROFOR commander - Smith conceded that at transcript page 7451 - who was well-known to have worked at the Ministry of Defence in London and engaged in conversations with NATO and the UN, that's Smith we're talking about, regarding the use of air-strikes against the VRS even prior to his arrival in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Transcript page 7371. Smith had evidence links to the US State Department, to whom he directly reported, bypassing his UN superiors and is highly suspected of having engaged in covert operations to destabilise the former Yugoslavia, evidenced in part by his refusal to answer questions on the matter, which were posed at transcript page 7367 through 8, and is expected to act in Bosnia with a clear mandate to "break the UNPROFOR machine and essentially pave the way for the international community to make war in BiH," as to declassified cables from Smith to the State Department talk about, D1462 and D452. Your Honours, I would now like to address the assertion by the Prosecution at paragraph 1041 of their final brief that the failure of the ABiH to separate civilians from military objects rendered SRK attacks on the ABiH in these positions unlawful. As I'm sure Your Honours are aware, the wording of Article 51(7) of AP I of the Geneva Conventions, the prohibition against human shields is widely understood to cover both the forcible movement of civilians to shield military objectives, as well as more subtle practices, such as deliberately placing a military objective in the middle of, or close to, a civilian area. This is arguable, particularly so if the civilians from that area are prohibited from leaving the area. Respectfully, the actions of the ABiH in positions themselves in civilian features falls squarely within this category. See, for example, paragraph 1838 to 1840 of our brief. Article 51(7) states in clear and unambiguous terms that: "Civilians shall not be used to render certain points or areas immune from military operations." Meaning that the SRK was not prohibited from engaging positions in which the ABiH were using human shields, as they did almost universally across Sarajevo. Holding a contrary legal position, Your Honours, would be tantamount to rewarding the ABiH for their use of human shields and could also encourage the use of human shields in future conflicts. Statements such as those referenced by the Prosecution at paragraph 1040 of their final brief should be interpreted in this context. In the face of this, the Chamber must recognise that the use of civilian features for military purposes, and the presence of the ABiH within them, extinguished the protections afforded these positions and thus allowed them to be engaged by the SRK, a principle articulated in the Kordic and Cerkez appeals judgement at paragraphs 455, 510, and 516. As per the Galic appeals judgement, this was true even of hospitals - paragraph 346 of that judgement - because of the regular presence of mobile mortars within their grounds. The lawfulness of attacks on these positions was therefore a question of proportionality, a topic for which the Prosecution has made grand overtures but little substantiated their claims and has failed to lead a single military expert on the topic. In fact, they have seemed abjectly afraid to dwell on the topic. I fear this is of their lack of any basic understanding of the principle of proportionality, as implied by their consistent reliance upon international witnesses who assert that the SRK used greater fire-power than the ABiH, and therefore acted disproportionately. As Your Honours are no doubt aware, the duty to proportionality does not oblige any equality of fire or tit-for-tat-type assaults, nor is it a matter of counting civilian casualties and comparing them to the number of any combatants put out of action. Rather, it is the obligation to protect against excessive collateral damage by using force only when the anticipated military advantage in using that force is proportionate to the collateral damage expected to result from it. It requires, in practical terms that those who plan or launch an attack consider the impact of their actions prior to engaging a target. The Defence has shown at paragraphs 1762 and 3 of our final brief that such considerations were required of each and every member of the SRK. What the Prosecution has not shown, as they are required to do, is that targets were then engaged despite the expectation there would be excessive collateral damage. On the contrary, Radojcic, for example, recalled giving up the fight for Dobrinjaska Street in 1993 because they noticed there were a large number of women and children there, and cancelling the assault on Butmir upon General Mladic's orders because they had confirmed information there were a large number of civilians, and any artillery fire would have caused heavy casualties among them. We find that at D535, paragraph 35. The same was true of the engagement of mobile mortars. The Prosecution have tried to convince you that shelling impacted on ostensibly civilian areas cannot be attributed to or justified by the engagement of mobile mortars. This is in paragraph 1039 of their final brief. But let me make perfectly clear, Your Honours, there were a good many military targets located in civilian areas. The Defence by no means suggests that these targets were limited to mobile mortars or, in the view and presence of these targets, engaged only mobile mortars in these areas. We've already talked about the Gotovina Appeals Chamber Judgement at paragraph 63 which found that mobile mortars were legitimate military targets and that the Trial Chamber had erred in finding that no shells were aimed at mobile military objects moving around town. This finding undermines the Prosecution's assertions that the engagement of mobile mortars by the SRK was, in and of itself, unlawful and that any attacks on the positions of departed mobile mortars were invalid. In fact, in accordance with their right to use force in self-defence, it was perfectly legitimate that the SRK would return fire in the face of an assault on their positions. Indeed, Witness Jordan confirmed such practice as standard operating procedure at transcript page 1818. When returning fire, it would be unlikely that those at the position attacked would have definitively known they had been assaulted by a mobile mortar for the simple fact that the effects emanating from mobile mortars are the same as those of stationary mortars. Transcript page 5532, 5506, 5493. Those at the position would have been aware only that the assault originated from a particular direction. It cannot be expected that they should have known they were engaged by mobile mortars before responding. In the midst of an attack, the decision to use force in self-defence is one made in necessary haste and often with little information on hand. This is different to the position of the proponent who would in all likelihood have access to a much wider range of information about their target, if only because they'd have had more time to plan and prepare this assault. As the Prosecution has alleged, it is indeed possible that the mobile mortar may have departed unbeknownst to their victim before they could respond, in a move commonly referred to as "shoot and scoot." This, however, does not necessarily mean that return fire of the SRK was unlawful. Indeed, the evidence shows that those who responded in such circumstances did so in pursuit of the significant military advantage that could be obtained by letting their opponents know they were aware of their positions and to intimidate the ABiH into stopping their attacks. Witness Draskovic, transcript page 38034. This undermines the Prosecution's assertions that such attacks were carried out simply to generate terror. In the Fuel Tanker Case, in Germany, from 2010, at pages 63 to 66, it was held that: "Considering the particular pressure at the moment when the decision had to be taken, an infringement is only to be assumed in cases of obvious excess where the commander ignored any considerations of proportionality and refrained from acting honestly, reasonably, and competently." The Prosecution has not evidenced that those who ordered the attacks on mobile mortars in Sarajevo or those who responded to attacks from mobile mortars in self-defence were negligent in this regard. In fact, they have not even evidenced that a single death or any form of collateral damage resulted from an attack on mobile mortars, whether or not it had departed. The actions of the SRK in attempting to engage mobile mortars cannot, therefore, be said to be disproportionate. This is so, even for those mobile mortars positioned on the grounds of the hospitals in Sarajevo. I'd like to briefly go into closed session -- pardon me, private session.

utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The Prosecution's allegations at paragraph 1042 of their final brief that they did is undermined by their referencing in the seam paragraph of witnesses who denied that mobile mortars were ever at the hospital, a claim rendered absurd by the overwhelming amount of evidence to the contrary. See paragraph 1766 of the Defence final brief. What's more, the evidence also demonstrates that return fire was targeted particularly at the mobile mortar, not the hospitals themselves, as attested to by Witnesses Mole and Segers, P421, paragraph 125; and D1465, page 11. In fact, in one incident witnessed by Segers at Kosevo Hospital, he noted that the SRK counter-fire upon the mobile mortar was very short - 43815, 43816 of the transcript - and that it resulted in no material substantive damage. Importantly, Segers also noted the practice of the SRK to warn before they returned fire, thus ensuring the lawfulness of their assaults in accordance with the Galic Appeals Chamber Judgement at paragraph 346. And, Your Honours, I see we're at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're at the time for a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would also have you believe that because a large number of shells were launched at Sarajevo at various times throughout the conflict, that these alleged bombardments must, ipso facto, have breached the principle of proportionality and selectivity. The fact remains that an attack or series of attacks which are extensive are not necessarily excessive or without military justification. The explanatory footnotes of the AP I suggests that: "Concrete and direct overall military advantage" refers to a military advantage that is foreseeable by the perpetrator at the relevant time. This includes advantages which may not necessarily be temporarily or geographically related to the object of the attack. In other words, the proportionality of an assault should be viewed in relation to the operation or conflict as a whole and the military objective therein. This approach has been adopted by a number of countries around the world, as evidenced in their respective military manuals, including - among other - as we now see on the screen: Canada, Australia, Germany, Italy, The Netherlands, New Zealand, UK, the US and - most importantly - the SFRY. The overarching military objective for the SRK was the complete cessation of hostilities in Sarajevo. In accordance with this, they acted pursuant only to a strategy of self-defence. They did not seek to take Sarajevo or advance their positions for any reason, other than to improve their ability to defend against the assaults of the ABiH. The Prosecution ignores this latter point in their final brief, particularly when discussing the Otes, Lukavac 93, and Pancir-2 operations in paragraphs 938 through 956 of the Prosecution final brief, and suggesting that their associated directives somehow evidence a common criminal plan. A proper assessment of proportionality requires an understanding of the objective with which an assault was launched: For the SRK, this was those two prior-mentioned objectives, the defence of their position and the complete cessation of hostilities. The "bombardment", for example, alleged in paragraph 779 of the Prosecution's brief, alleged to have taken place on 21 March 1993, is actually evidenced to have been a legitimate act of self-defence against an intense ABiH assault on a key SRK supply route on the Pale-Lukavica road. RM176 testified about that. As their key supply route, the road was of significant importance to the SRK and their ability to affect the defence of their positions. The neighbourhoods alleged to have been impacted by this bombardment all contained key military targets. Witnesses Sehovac, Sladoje, Dzino, among other evidence, talks about that. In the face of the difficulties of the SRK would have faced in defending their positions had the ABiH attack been successful, the intense but short-lived shelling of these targets was evidently proportionate. No collateral is, after all, evidenced to have occurred -- that is to say, no collateral damage is, after all, evidenced to have occurred. Incidents G1 and G2 are evidence of the SRK acting pursuant to their objective to bring a permanent resolution to the conflict in Sarajevo. In implementing the G1 campaign: "All military targets that were in the area of Sarajevo were part of the plan for combat." We see that evidence at transcript page 4990. Mladic's orders were understood to apply only to valid military targets, many of which were located in the old town, where according to Prosecution Witness Wilson: "The weight of fire seemed to be going." Transcript page 3970. No evidence beyond this is led that any non-military targets were deliberately engaged. In the context of the consistent and enduring attacks by the ABiH on SRK positions, the failure to negotiate peace by political and diplomatic means and the expressed intent of Izetbegovic to continue the conflict in Sarajevo, almost at all costs, it surely can be understood that a complete cessation of hostilities could not have been achieved in Sarajevo without the use of considerable force. However, the cessation of hostilities would not only have enabled the SRK to fulfil their objective in Sarajevo but would also have saved countless lives and millions of dollars on all sides of the confrontation. The military advantage anticipated was therefore considerable. Intense and prolonged assaults of this nature have been used by countless armies around the world to achieve their objectives. Such assaults are often referred to as shock and awe or "rapid dominance." That -- we'd like to go into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Given the forward-looking nature of the principle of proportionality, the failure of the SRK to achieve their anticipated advantage does not render the assault unlawful. This is again from the Fuel Tanker Case we discussed earlier, page 63 to 66. Nor, in fact, does it evidence the charge of terror. In light of the fact that there were -- that each assault was justified militarily, whether because they were acts of defence against an immediate threat, repositioning to improve their defences against an expected threat, or attempts to end the conflict and eliminate the threat altogether, the SRK cannot be said to have acted for the primary purpose of inflicting terror amongst the civilian population of Sarajevo. I will now turn to the use of modified aerial bombs in Sarajevo. The Prosecution has alleged that the use of modified aerial bomb in the latter years of the war was particularly disproportionate. However, on the contrary, when deciding on the proportionality of an attack, those planning, launching, or responding to assaults are entitled to take into account the current weapon stocks and future supply requirements of their army. The evidence tells us that at the time modified aerial bombs were employed, the SRK suffered an acute shortage of artillery and weaponry, D486, D686, D535. Given their limited stock, the sole use of mortar would have depleted their stock to such a degree that they had no effective defence against ABiH assaults. This was a particular consideration because despite what the Prosecution would have you believe, the evidence shows that the ABiH had some considerably stronger -- had become considerably stronger and better armed throughout the conflict, D468, paragraphs 17 to 19. Without a variety of mortar and artillery available to them, it was believed that the ABiH could and would breach SRK lines and massacre the civilians living in SRK territory, D468. The preservation of a variety was therefore of significant importance and military advantage to the ability of the SRK to defend against the attacks of the ABiH. It was for this reason and no other that modified aerial bombs were designed, constructed, and ultimately used by the SRK in Sarajevo. They were not - as the Prosecution has alleged - introduced in order to terrorise the civilian population of Sarajevo and they were not - as was also alleged by the Prosecution - amateurly designed, imprecise weapons, improvised by the SRK. Indeed, even the Prosecution at paragraphs 1005 and 1006 of their final brief concede that the modified aerial bombs were designed by experts; constructed at one of the largest special-purpose weapons production factors in the former Yugoslavia, Pretis; and subjected to extensive testing prior to their distribution and use. The modified air bomb were also accompanied by a detailed firing table, a firing table, it should be noted, that the Prosecution repeatedly denied in their desperate attempt to substantiate their allegations against General Mladic even though it was shown to have existed. To this end, Your Honours, the use of the modified aerial bombs cannot be said to be either disproportionate or unlawful. Your Honours, I would now like to draw your attention to the allegation by the Prosecution that the indiscriminate shelling of Sarajevo is evidenced by the occasional impact of one or two shells in the residential areas of Sarajevo, for example, paragraph 778 of their brief; and the allegation that unlawful sniping is evidenced by the deaths of civilians by gun-fire. It should be noted from the outset that the Prosecution has not provided any evidence which demonstrates that such shells were wilfully launched at these areas by the SRK or those shots made wilfully against civilians. This is particularly so, given that it is a known fact that the accuracy of any weapon is affected by a number of factors, including weather and atmospheric condition, Witness Hamill, transcript page 5525. And that natural, unavoidable, variations occur between weapons, even those of the same type and make. This should be borne in mind when analysing incidents such as G6, in which the Prosecution have alleged that the SRK fired three rounds at Geteova Street and Bosanska Street in Alipasino Polje, completely ignoring the fact that the Prosecution's own witness admitted that the ABiH's Kulin Ban barracks was located on the other side of the building from where the mortar impacted. This was at transcript page 4293. And the Prosecution counsel demonstrated apparent ignorance by asking if the witness personally knew Mr. Kulin Ban. The Kulin Ban barracks stood a mere 150 metres away, as visualised in D82. This is well within the accepted beaten zone of a mortar system, as testified to by Prosecution Witness Hamill. The majority of damage which occurred to civilian objects in Sarajevo occurred on or near the front line. Only a comparatively small degree of damage occurred without apparent military justification away from these areas, P640, page 16. The Prosecution has not evidenced that General Mladic wilfully ordered the shelling of these positions or that the SRK deliberately engaged them. As such, the Prosecution cannot claim that these unintended impacts of both artillery and gun-fire, if caused by the SRK at all, were not the result of weather conditions, faults in the weaponry, or natural variations between the weaponry. SRK assaults on Sarajevo cannot, therefore, reasonably be considered unlawful or made in the pursuit of terror merely because a small number of sniping or shelling incidents are alleged to have impacted on non-military targets. Arguably, in fact, the city of Sarajevo itself consisted a valid military target in its entirety. As the Court is undoubtedly already aware, Article 3(c) of the ICTY's Statute as well as general international law prohibits attacks or bombardments by whatever means of undefended cities. Nevertheless, Sarajevo does not qualify as an undefended city due to the substantially spread out military activities occurring throughout that city. Under the military manuals and national practice of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the SFRY, in order for a city to be undefended, it must have been recognised as such by the parties or if must fulfil certain conditions such as lack of armed forces and activities of a military nature. We see this from both the 1992 BiH military instructions and the 1988 SFRY military manual. International law dictates that the respective city must have been recognised by the belligerent parties as "open" or, alternatively, that it must fulfil concern preconditions such as lack of a defence and any armed forces. This comes from multiple military manuals, including the UK, Canada, Australia, Belgium, Germany, and the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As is already known, Sarajevo was the scene of strenuous and long-lasting combat. The imposition of the 1994 -- Your Honours, I'm told that the translation has ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The imposition of the 1994 demilitarisation agreement in Sarajevo having failed, there was never any agreement as to the status of Sarajevo as an open city. On the contrary, as much as the Prosecution may not like it, the evidence shows that the city was at all times occupied by ABiH personnel and with a significant number of military objects, thus rendering Sarajevo a defended city. Furthermore, the strategic location of Sarajevo, its industrial capacity, and its very nature indisputably confer an effective contribution to military actions. It is the capital and the biggest urban settlement in BiH which, ipso facto, renders its destruction, capture, or neutralisation a definite military advantage. Moreover, the neutralisation of the BiH troops present in the city offers an incontestable military advantage. Consequently, Sarajevo fulfils the requirements for a legitimate military object looking at Article 52(2) of Additional Protocol I, 1977, and it makes the ABiH's refusal to allow people to leave the city all and their use of human shields all the more horrific. As such, directing attacks toward it is was indeed lawful and the accused cannot be held accountable for carrying out his responsibilities, as the general of the army, within the boundaries of the law. All that we have discussed this morning leads to the conclusion, Your Honours, that there was no criminal plan designed or implemented in Sarajevo, let alone a modulation of any supposed campaign which was used to leverage the accord of the Bosnian Muslim leadership. Despite the attempts of the Prosecution to have you believe otherwise and their deliberate omissions of the context, the evidence shows us that the actions of the SRK were militarily justified: They were responding to the assaults of the ABiH, improving their defensive positions, and trying to bring about a conclusive end to the conflict in Sarajevo. In light of this, they cannot be said to have undertaken for the primary purpose of inflicting terror upon the civilian population of Sarajevo. There was no ratcheting up or ratcheting down. In fact, the times ratcheting alleged by the Prosecution accord with only one of the major agreements negotiated throughout the conflict, an agreement which incidentally was rescinded by Alija Izetbegovic, hardly evidence of well-modulated, drawn-out campaigns through which the VRS and RS manipulate others into acting in accordance with their wishes. The Prosecution has neither evidenced any link between this supposed ratcheting and the progress of the conflict in other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In what way, therefore, was Sarajevo used as a lever? In fact, the Prosecution case is so weak that they have not even been able to evidence any linkage between the SRK and the peaks in shelling and various assaults alleged by the Prosecution in paragraphs 770, 777, and 797 of their final brief. In view of the overwhelming evidence demonstrating the ABiH's propensity to self-target, it cannot be alleged on any sound basis that these peaks are evidence of the SRK or General Mladic's modulation of the conflict. Indeed, it is highly possible that these peaks and troughs were illustrative only of the ordinary course of wars. The allegation that humanitarian aid was restricted or forbidden without cause and that this was part of some ploy to spread terror or use Sarajevo as leverage is, to use the language of the Prosecution, a mere conspiracy theory. In referencing the Defence brief at transcript page 44502, Mr. Weber selectively omitted to address the substantial amount of evidence which demonstrates the widespread and pervasive abuse of the airport and humanitarian aid convoys to smuggle in weapons, ammunition, and military goods for the ABiH. And the evidence which shows that once these illicit goods were removed and sometimes even in spite of the presence of these illicit good, humanitarian aid was permitted to continue. In fact, an UNHCR investigation undertaken in 1993 found that over 2500 tonnes of food had been stockpiled, only a fraction of which was reaching the civilians, a situation which changed little throughout the war; a 1994 report finding less than a third of the aid brought into the city actually reached civilians. D8, page 3; P7779, page 3. It is preposterous to suggest that the accused could somehow be responsible for hoarding of aid by the BiH side. Similarly, given the evidenced attacks of the ABiH on the supply of gas, water, and electricity into Sarajevo, any periods of disruption are attributable as much to the actions of the ABiH than any other; and as such, do little to evidence the Prosecution's claim that General Mladic modulated the supply of these services as a form of leverage. Your Honours, I could spend consider time going through the 16th Assembly speech which the Prosecution has primarily relied upon to evidence the general's supposed intent to engage in a common criminal plan, but we have spent time on this already; and given this, I will not repeat that evidence. As discussed in the JCE section, Karadzic was the supreme commander of the VRS and, consequently, the SRK. Mladic was subordinate to him. In accordance with the culture and the ethos of both the military and the Serbian people, Mladic could not and would not publicly disagree with his supreme commander. Rather, these conversations occurred behind closed doors, but despite this there is significant evidence to demonstrate that disagreements between Mladic and Karadzic, in fact, did occur P1469, page 2. The same is true of Mladic's relationship with his subordinates, particularly Galic and Milosevic. Indeed, in P1052, page 7 through 8, it is noted that Karadzic and Krajisnik would often call on Milosevic to come and see them to plan operations in Sarajevo. Krajisnik and Karadzic, it was said at page 26 to 27 of the same document, did not spend much time in the Main Staff often, nor did they invite the general to meetings or other broader-based gatherings. Karadzic's and Krajisnik's attitudes towards the Army of Republika Srpska is illustrated by their direct contacts and invitations to General Milosevic, commander of the SRK. On many occasions Milosevic responded to those invitations for which he was reprimanded by Mladic, who even warned him that he was forbidden to go and talk to Karadzic and Krajisnik without his approval. Because of such behaviours by Karadzic and Krajisnik, Mladic got into arguments with them as well and pointed out that officers subordinated to him could not be summoned without his knowledge. The content of those talks between Karadzic, Krajisnik, and General Milosevic is not known. General Mladic can hardly be said to be acting in collusion with those who deliberately excluded him from their operational planning. To borrow a phrase from my learned colleague

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Scratch the surface of the Prosecution's allegations and it falls apart. The Prosecution talks of murder and unlawful attacks and terror, and in doing so they make broad, uncontextualised allegations that do little to prove the elements of these crimes. They hope to bamboozle you with numbers and figures and images which will invoke your sympathies and cover the fact that they have not met the burden of proof required for the charges they have alleged. They attempt this most predominantly by evincing videos, images, and accounts of the horrors that people experienced throughout this conflict. When viewing these images and hearing these testimonies, it is impossible as a human not to feel something in reaction and to feel compelled to leap to a conclusion based upon that feeling. And it's easy to forget in the midst of that, that these images predominantly depict only one perspective of the conflict, that from inside Sarajevo, where - incidentally - most of the international personnel and media were stationed. These images and videos and testimonies do not capture the conflict in Sarajevo in its totality. They do not show the full picture. The evidence presented in this case does not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the SRK of General Mladic allowed for or undertook any unlawful attacks. It does not show that terror was intended or that the death of any person in Sarajevo was the result of deliberate actions of either the SRK or General Mladic. It does not show a JCE existed or that the conflict in Sarajevo was modulated for use as some imaginary level for RS, Republika Srpska, to get what it wanted out of its political negotiations. What it does show is that the SRK and General Mladic fought in defence of their homes, their lives, and their right for every ethnicity to be treated as equals, both politically and socially. It shows the difficult position -- the difficult decisions that both the general and his men faced on a daily basis and their efforts to protect themselves and their families from incessant assaults of the ABiH and a political leader - Izetbegovic - who would sacrifice all for his gain. Now I wish to move to the Srebrenica part of the case, where various parts of the indictment allegation everything from forcible transfers, persecutions, to genocide. We believe that a considerable amount of reasonable doubt exists to what happened and why in Srebrenica. While this Defence does not deny that a certain number of men and boys were tragically killed in acts of personal revenge at Srebrenica, these killings have nothing - nothing - to do with any orders or intentions of General Mladic. Sadly, the Prosecution chose not to investigate Srebrenica in a proper manner, and we thus will never know the full truth, nor ascertain the true number of persons killed in crimes, as opposed to legitimate deaths from combat, attempted escapes, and other circumstances from the years prior that are included in the Prosecution's figure. Rather than seeking truth and reconciliation, Mr. McCloskey urged you to "strike back" at Mr. Mladic for these crimes. This was at transcript 44526. Respectfully, I don't believe the mandate of this Tribunal is based upon vigilanteism and revenge; rather, it is supposed to be justice and truth. Only the proper application of justice and truth can try to heel the wounds of Srebrenica and lead to reconciliation and peace. The truth is that we will never know if all these tragic events from July 1995 could have been avoided. Arguably, had the international community - including the United Nations but especially the United States - acted in good faith as to the demilitarisation of Srebrenica and had Naser Oric's ABiH troops in Srebrenica laid down their arms or departed either in 1993, 1994, or even 1995, the situation would be different, but they did not. Demilitarisation was an illusion and a lie in a tragic play which saw only Ratko Mladic adhering in good faith to demilitarization and seeking peace in the Srebrenica area, while the United Nations turned a blind eye to its obligations to enforce demilitarisation against the ABiH and the United States actively assisted the troops of Naser Oric to violate the agreement and resupply their arms. We saw through the evidence that the ABiH turned over only antique and non-functioning weapons, while hiding its true armaments and forces in the Srebrenica enclave, from where they conducted vicious and barbaric attacks against surrounding Serb villages killing over 1,300 Serbs in the years prior to 1995. General Mladic continually pleaded with the UN to enforce the demilitarisation of Srebrenica and for a complete cessation of hostilities as to the area. Look at D944, D1665. But apparently only General Mladic was engaged in genuinely seeking the attainment of peace. Everyone else was intent on the sham demilitarisation and the myth that Srebrenica was a protected area. Do not blame and strike back at General Mladic - as sought by the Prosecution - for the failings and malfeasance of others, including politicians and Bosnian Muslim officials and the SDA. They share the blame with those that perpetrated the killings in Srebrenica, the killings on both sides, prior to 1995 and in July 1995, not Ratko Mladic. He does not have that blame. The Prosecution's narrative would ignore and deny what even Prosecution witnesses like Momir Nikolic talked about, discussing the desire of local Serbs for revenge for Oric's crimes as being palpable in 1995, transcript page 34930. Such tendency for revenge was confirmed by Prosecution investigator Ruez, 10417. Military expert Kovac also talked of that as a cause of the Srebrenica killings, transcript page 41395. Oric's crimes do not excuse the revenge killings in 1995, but they do explain them and demonstrate why persons would act contrary to any orders of General Mladic to safe-guard the POWs. Further, the Prosecution narrative ignores the fact under law - which we have just discussed - that Srebrenica was also a defended city. Thus, its status as a protected area was nullified because of the failure of the ABiH to demilitarise. GRM097 testified that a failure to disarm released the Serb side from obligations under the agreements as to Srebrenica, as they had a right to self-defence from ABiH attacks. Witness Akashi told us that the Secretary-General of the UN complained of the flaws and failures of the UN protected area regime to the UN Security Council to no avail, including the failure to demilitarise the enclave and that the ABiH was continuing to militarily use Srebrenica to stage attacks. None of the actions of the VRS undertaken in the lead-up to the Krivaja 95 operation can be understood as evidencing a criminal intent to commit genocide or otherwise, because the alternative conclusion is available under evidence to conclude that such actions were legitimate responses to the attacks and encroachment of the ABiH forces from Srebrenica and the failure to demilitarise which rendered Srebrenica a defended city. Again, Prosecution expert Butler and Mr. McCloskey have conceded that even the very operation of Krivaja 95 is a legitimate military aim; and therefore, Your Honours, it cannot be used as evidence of a crime. We saw that last Friday with a PowerPoint, where I showed you their positions on that from the record. And now, despite that, in the final brief of the Prosecution at paragraph 1116 the Prosecution presents a new theory, namely, that Krivaja 95 was meant to force humanitarian conditions, forcing people to leave. And we heard already last week how the Prosecution tried to misrepresent the Fontana meetings, contrary to the evidence and conclusions of Mr. Butler. Don't let them do that. Once they've said something is not illegal and not criminal, they can't go back and claim it is. Thus far, we have demonstrated in our submissions that the Prosecution position seeks to disavow and defeat no fewer than three of their own expert witnesses on military matters. The Defence cannot stress enough that the Prosecution has conceded through their expert Richard Butler that not a single order of General Mladic has been found which orders any of the killings alleged as to Srebrenica. For the record, he said that at transcript page 16573. Your Honours, that is pretty compelling of reasonable doubt and acquittal right there. Such a result, acquittal, becomes all the more necessary the more you review the Prosecution evidence. And as a preliminary matter, last week it was suggested that the Mladic Defence is blaming General Krstic for the crimes of Srebrenica; nothing can be farther from the truth. It is not our job to accuse anyone, nor prove anyone's guilt. Last week the Prosecution showed several videos of Potocari to demonstrate how "images that speak for themselves" of people fleeing. This was at transcript page 44536 and 44537. Yet, the images that you were shown were craftily edited, such that in one segment you were shown a vast image of civilians, but General Mladic speaking and addressing them was cut out by the Prosecution, as was the expressions of gratitude towards General Mladic from this crowd of people. We will see those missing clips later in this presentation. But now I want to take a step back and first respond to the allegations of forcible transfer. Last week, Mr. McCloskey said, and now I quote him from transcript page 44537: "The idea that these people voluntarily left is insulting." Strong words. I dare say, then, that whatever insulting behaviour upset Mr. McCloskey, it is misplaced if he looks at my client for the reason they left. Nothing can be farther from the truth. But let's take a look at Mr. McCloskey's own evidence on this topic, because again he is the one with the burden of proof; and his own evidence demonstrates Mr. Mladic cannot be blamed for any of the forcible transfers from Srebrenica. In fact, Prosecution evidence demonstrates that it was first the BiH command in Srebrenica themselves who decided to abandon Srebrenica and directed the civilians would go to Potocari, to the UN base there, whereas the males would start off in a military formation and set out from Susnjari and try to break through the Serb lines, Prosecution Witness RM253; Prosecution Exhibit P1547, paragraph 2. If there is a need to be insulted, the rage should therefore be against the Bosnian Muslim leadership, not Mladic. My client cannot be held responsible for the acts of these persons. This is either evidence of a voluntarily departure or the SDA and ABiH forcing their own people to go. Either way, General Mladic is not to blame. If we can have the slide on the screen. By the way, P1462 - admitted in this case as the 92 ter statement of Witness Malagic - is an expert from her testimony in the Tolimir case, where Mr. McCloskey himself elicited the following testimony at pages 12 to 13 in e-court: "Q. And describe to us what happened there, what was going on now again as best as can you recall but ... "A. My older brother, my husband, and my sons decided at that moment with other able-bodied men that they could reach Tuzla on foot, so they simply went towards the free territory. They were looking for a way out. They did not dare to go to Potocari. They told us women and children and the infirm to go towards Potocari, telling us that the UNPROFOR was going to protect us. They were not able to take the same route." Again, the evidence led by Mr. McCloskey does not evidence Mr. Mladic telling people where to go. The Bosnian Muslims decided for themselves. By the way, the Prosecution's final trial brief concedes at paragraph 1161 that Colonel Karremans of DutchBat asked General Mladic to approve departure of both DutchBat and the civilians from Potocari because the civilians of Srebrenica wanted to go. The brief says they wanted to go. Pay attention to what the Prosecution has conceded - reasonable doubt - and therefore, this is case is worthy of acquittal. If now we have also in evidence Prosecution Witness Franken and D280 is the statement he gave to the Dutch Ministry of Defence, page 6 of which has been excerpted in the slide that we have before us. And we see here it says: "Regarding refugee transport, it was agreed with Mladic that UNPROFOR would supervise it. Our role was to provide as much presence as possible and to escort them. The men were separated from the women. The Muslims agreed to let the men be investigated for war crimes, under the supervision of the UNHCR and the Red Cross." And then we have: "NB: Franken says he is in the possession of the English and Bosnian text of the agreement with Mladic. He himself proceeded on the basis of an oral translation by the interpreter." From this evidence, one can conclude a totally benign status of refugee transport, not deportation nor forcible transfer. Reasonable doubt means acquittal. Then if we look at the entirety of the context, it is clear that the UN personnel, both inside and outside Srebrenica, determined that a humanitarian evacuation, not a deportation, not a forcible transfer, of civilians from Potocari was a necessity. Among others, we heard Generals Nicolai, major Franken, and Colonel Boering all attest to that fact under oath in the courtroom; and again, they used the word "evacuation." Documentary evidence of the VRS demonstrates that what was intended and understood from their side was, again, an evacuation and that terminology was used. Look at P1714, for instance. Respectfully, the Prosecution hopes by referring to these events as forcible removal or deportation that they can ignore and overcome the plethora of evidence to the contrary. I propose now to take a look now at P1165, the witness statement of Prosecution Witness General Cornelius Nicolai taken by the Prosecution in 1996 and paragraph 59 of the same. If we can have the next slide. Again, if the Prosecution feels insulted by what is said in here, that feeling of insult was not shown when this document was tendered by the Prosecution. Looking at this particular paragraph of the statement it says here: "Colonel Karremans commenced negotiations with General Mladic that night, and I was advised for the first time that Mladic was on the grouped there. The next day, the negotiations were to continue with Mladic. We were instructing Colonel Karremans on what he had to do during these [sic] negotiations - these negotiations by telephone and in writing. We instructed him to stay with the civilian population so that he and his men could observe the evacuation in order that it would be carried out within the international rules. Directly after we stopped the air attacks, we realised that the civilian population would have to be evacuated from Srebrenica. There was no food, enough medical care, or even protection from the weather for the people there. We had hoped to do this under the cover of the UNPROFOR troops and even use UNPROFOR trucks, if necessary. On the 11th of July, I had informed the Dutch minister of defence of the planned evacuation and our intention to use UNPROFOR trucks and he had agreed to this." What is clear from this is that UNPROFOR, after it stopped the air attacks, decided it must evacuate the civilians from Srebrenica. There was not a consultation with Mladic before they decided this. It was that the UN that decided before Karremans even met with General Mladic. Again, if we are to view the departure of civilians from Srebrenica as a crime, as part of a JCE, then the Prosecution's own evidence implicates that this crime would have to be hatched by UNPROFOR, by the Dutch minister of defence, and by the Dutch Chief of Staff of BH command, not by General Ratko Mladic. And let's recall that General Nicolai was rather honest about this when he testified here. If we can -- yeah. "Q. And, thus, I suppose, sir, that the instructions and orders you sent to Colonel Karremans before he met with General Mladic for the first time would have dealt with the elevation and the need for the refugees to be evacuated; am I correct? "A. Yes. That was -- I no longer needed to explain the necessity of this to Colonel Karremans. He could readily understand this, and it was also simply an order from UNPROFOR to Colonel Karremans that the evacuation would have to take place. However, naturally, we did have to inform him as to how we supposed this might take place before -- because for the execution we needed the co-operation of the Bosnian Serb forces, where he had to negotiate that on the spot." And, Your Honours, I think we're at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are, Mr. Ivetic. Thank you for reminding me. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at 15 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I neglected to mention the transcript page of the selection I just read out for General Nicolai. It is transcript page 10654 of our transcript and it's been brought to my attention at temporary transcript page 7, line 13, I used "PTT building" when I should have used "RTV building" when referring to Mr. Weber's comments from the other day. And now I'll continue. So from this testimony of Nicolai we see that Colonel Karremans was ordered by his UN superiors to negotiate for what the UN wanted, which was the co-operation of the VRS to get the Bosnian Muslim civilians out of Potocari. Again, if there is a criminal order for any removal of people from Srebrenica, it does not bear Mr. Mladic's signature; it bears an UN stamp. If we can go to the next slide. Then we have the Prosecution's own trial video, P1147, and here we have a portion from the transcript dealing with Mr. Karremans and this is Mr. Karremans speaking in the video: "Then I asked for a -- let's say, a team from the UNHCR and civil authorities which can deliver us the means, like buses. The only thing I can do is studying the amount of persons and for that amount of person, we need, let's say, transport. Counting. But if it's possible, I can ask for buses through my own authorities, let's say military authorities, but I really don't know what they can give me. I don't know yet. We are busy with determining which -- which people like to go where, but that needs time, and I don't -- I don't know, of course, what is possible in that -- in that way. But I presume that that something which Mr. Mandzic can tell. I don't know where they'd like to go. Then we make a -- let's say, a plan for evacuation which persons do need to go first because of age, illness, et cetera." Now, again, I notice no one is using the word "deportation" nor "forcible transfer." It's always "evacuation." Mr. Mandzic was mentioned, you will recall, is a representative of the Bosnian Muslim civilians themselves. So again we have here an alternate, reasonable conclusion under the evidence, that the Bosnian Muslim civilians were voluntarily determining where they wanted to go. Reasonable doubt exists and acquittal is warranted. If we can go to the next slide. Now, Colonel Boering of DutchBat likewise testified and just after having watched this very same segment of the Srebrenica trial video which we just read from the transcript of, he testified as follows at transcript page 10067 to 10068: "A. We prepared the second meeting. We discussed various organisations who might possibly offer support, then requests to go to Tuzla, Sarajevo. These requests -- we also discussed various organisations, but a real plan? That's something I cannot recollect in detail. It was more in -- in general. We mentioned organisations and a way to get out of it. "Q. Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans says that drafting any evacuation plan would involve establishing the priorities of those people who wanted to leave. When you were preparing for this meeting, did you ever discuss priorities and how they would be determined? "A. Yes, I can remember that we discussed this, that we were going to transfer the wounded first and then the elderly and then, at the final stage, the healthy people. So there were some priorities set there. But I don't know how much detail we went when establishing it all." So, Your Honours, from this we see requests were being received to go to Tuzla and Sarajevo and recall from the evidence that these were both ABiH-held areas. So again, people are voluntarily selecting where to go. Now let's finally get to what Mr. Mladic actually said on the topic. We saw last week the third Fontana meeting that nothing improper was suggested in that meeting. Again, expert Butler told us about that, and I'd like to go to the next slide. This is an encounter between Mr. Koster and Mr. Mladic from the Srebrenica trial video, Eelco Koster of DutchBat; and this is misrepresented by the Prosecution at paragraph 1200 and 629 of their brief. Now, as to the video, Your Honours will recall - and you see it in the transcript of the video - that the realtime translation received by Mr. Koster by the translator on site in Potocari is incorrect and misinterprets General Mladic as essentially saying that they would board everyone on the buses, when in fact during our trial and with the revised Srebrenica trial video, this translation was corrected to reflect what General Mladic really said, which is: "We will board everyone who wants it." Now, this incident gives us several things to think about. DutchBat members on the ground, based upon this clearly faulty translation, cannot be relied upon to correctly describe General Mladic's words and therefore his intent because we cannot exclude the possibility that this same faulty translator messed up other words of General Mladic that are not recorded on film for which we don't have the ability to go back and check now but which DutchBat members like Leandert van Duijn had in their mind and testified about. But another thing strikes me about this mistranslation. The mistranslation resembles the purported intercept P1236 cited by the Prosecution. And again, for that intercept there's no recording of Mladic allegedly saying what is there and albeit it's in the Croatian, not the Serbian language, which raises other doubts. But that intercept, in essence, says that the Serbs would evacuate those that wanted to and those did not. So given that this tape with the updated and corrected translation only came in existence recently, can we exclude the possibility of someone at the ABiH or perhaps an international agency doctoring and faking intercepts to fit the accusations of forcible transfer against Mladic, relying on the prior version of the tape with the faulty translation or perhaps hoping that the faulty translation would be used to support the authenticity of that intercept? Because I can't remove that possibility from my mind. Again, reasonable doubt. Now, let's look at the other footage from Potocari which the Prosecution edited out of its presentation last week. I would ask to go to the next slide. The transcripts have been provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] "Mladic: Anyone who wishes to be transported will be transported, be the person small, big, old, or young. "The Crowd: Thank you. Thank you. "Mladic: Don't be afraid ... slowly, slowly. Let the women and children go first. Thirty business will arrive and we will transport you towards Kladanj. From there, you will pass onto the territory controlled by Alija's forces. Just don't panic and let the little children and the women go first. Be careful not to lose a child. Do not be afraid. Nobody will harm you. "The Crowd: Thank you. Thank you. "Man From the Crowd: May you live long. "Journalist: General, after the liberation of Srebrenica, there are several thousand Muslim civilians who are located here. What will become of them? "Mladic: Well, I have received the representatives of this population here today and they have asked me to enable the civilians who want to leave this territory to cross over into the territory controlled by Muslims and Croats. Our army wasn't aiming to fight the civilians or the UNPROFOR forces. We have organised transport for them, food, water and medicine. In the first round today, we will evacuate women, children, and the elderly, as well as other people who want to leave this combat zone of their own free will, without any coercion." "Mladic: How old are you? "Boy: 12. "Mladic: Please be patient. Anybody who wishes to stay, can stay. Anybody who wishes to leave this territory can leave this territory.
