utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So just to make clear, we just heard General Mladic repeat that people had a choice to stay or to go, just as he told civilian representatives at the third Hotel Fontana meeting. The gathered Bosnian Muslim civilians are heard to express gratitude and bless General Mladic for his words and behaviour towards them. This is the very same General Mladic who sits before you today and who patiently and with great discomfort had to listen to the Prosecution's hurtful accusations last week. If anyone in this courtroom deserves to feel insulted by the insinuations of forcible removals, it is General Mladic. For Your Honours, as we have seen, the decision to have people leave Srebrenica was made first and foremost by the inhabitants of Srebrenica themselves and by the ABiH forces therein. Then the UN ordered that they be evacuated and tasked Colonel Karremans to present this as a complete plan -- as a fait accompli to General Mladic and asked for help for a humanitarian evacuation. General Mladic agreed to help and personally undertook to mobilise buses on short order. How can one conclude from this evidence that everyone who planned and ordered the departures and presented them to Mladic is a saint and Mladic is to be the devil, guilty of the crime of forcible transfers? We just cannot accept that. Not unless, again, it is the Serbs that are guilty even for things that are called "humanitarian" if do you them and you're not a Serb. However, if do you not believe this, an acquittal is required. Now I'd like to shift gears a bit and talk about the so-called JCE to eliminate or murder the men of Srebrenica. I've already mentioned that Mr. McCloskey made up the story about the dinner between Krstic and Mladic in calm surroundings. He described it, et cetera, the other day in his closing. Let's look at what they actually said in the Prosecution final brief. This is paragraphs 1063 and 1105. Let's look at the first one first. "Sometime between the evening of 11 July and the morning of 12 July, Mladic and other JCE members developed concrete plans to detain and summarily execute large numbers of Muslim men and boys and forcibly transport to BiH territory of women and children of Srebrenica." How telling is this? After all this, the Prosecution concedes it does not even know when the plan was created. So again, this cute little fantasy of a dinner, is all made up. Reasonable doubt exists; an acquittal is mandated. Now let's look at the second paragraph on this slide, also from the Prosecution brief, 1105. I'm going to read the highlighted portion: "Up until that point, the objective was to permanently forcibly remove the Bosnian Muslim population from Srebrenica. Soon after Mladic and the other JCE members became aware of the large number of men and boys in Potocari, a JCE was created with the common criminal purpose of eliminating Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica." At paragraph 1175, the Prosecution says that this happened sometime between the evening of 11 July and the third Hotel Fontana meeting at 10.00 a.m. on the 12th of the July. So in their final brief, Your Honours, the Prosecution concedes that there can be no JCE to kill but for this mysterious meeting that they cannot locate any evidence about but that they're sure happened. By the way, this means what I told you last week is true. The statement of Mr. Mladic to the camera as he's still in Srebrenica, the one talking about "it's time to take revenge on the Turks" cannot be tied to any JCE to commit genocide or kill, since it predates this mysterious meeting between the evening of 11 July and 12 July that the Prosecution says is the actual start date for that JCE. Remember, reasonable doubt mandates acquittal. Now let's try to find this mysterious meeting where everyone had to talk about and decide to form into this JCE to eliminate, because without this meeting the Prosecution's case is lost. Paragraph 1175 of the Prosecution brief says: "In deciding to kill the able-bodied men in Potocari, Mladic would have consulted with Krstic and his senior intelligence and security offers present in Bratunac, Popovic, Keserovic, and Jankovic." And then to support that allegation they have a footnote relating to VRS testimony of General Milovanovic. Unfortunately, none of those several references to General Milovanovic's testimony say anything about this which is cited in the Prosecution's brief. Again, the Prosecution makes up its case when it doesn't have the evidence. Various evidence of the meeting held at the Fontana hotel on the evening of 11 July 1995 provides for the reasonable conclusion that no such criminal plan was discussed nor agreed to at this meeting. To start with, it should be noted that even the Prosecution's star insider witness, Momir Nikolic, fails to allege that anything criminal was discussed at this meeting on the 11th. Nikolic was not present, but he saw the accused, General Krstic, the commanders of the groups of each brigade who were participating in the Srebrenica operation, so Pandurevic, Blagojevic, Tribic, Andric. According to Momir Nikolic this meeting took place around 1700 or 1800 hours when it was still light before the meeting at the Fontana hotel on the same day, and we get that from D1228. Afterwards, Nikolic found out from Blagojevic about what was said at the meeting, namely, that the Srebrenica operation was analysed and there was a conflict between Blagojevic and Krstic because they disagreed on the Bratunac Brigade's participation and then a discussion about the Zepa operation started and Pandurevic did not want to start Zepa until the column of the 28th Division had been dealt with. So again, Nikolic can't provide evidence of a meeting where crimes were discussed. Several witnesses testified that they were present for or heard of a meeting that same evening, the 11th, where nothing criminal was discussed and, rather, the plans for Zepa were discussed, which is again what Nikolic says was discussed. These are Colonel Andric, D1033, paragraph 19; Milenko Jevdjevic, transcript page 32059 onwards; Miodrag Dragutinovic, who told us that Pandurevic discussed the meeting with him, transcript page 32241 to 32242. The Prosecution claims that all these witnesses are lying and that the meeting that they are talking about actually took place on 12 July, based solely on P1467, the diary of a Colonel Trivic that has a meeting on 12 July which is similar in nature. It is interesting, however, that in saying that everyone is lying, the Prosecution does not include Momir Nikolic and never addresses his testimony that nothing criminal was discussed on the evening of 11 July. But there's one problem with that position, Your Honours. The Prosecution says everyone is to be disbelieved, but the diary, the diary is said to be credible, reliable, written in great detail and precision and accurate. And that's at paragraph 1216 of their final brief. But this very same diary has no meeting on the 11th of July nor at any time where any JCE to kill the inhabitants of Srebrenica is discussed. So where is the this affirmative proof establishing beyond reasonable doubt the meeting, the genesis of their JCE is alleged? Simply put, they do not present any. Irrespective of the dates, no evidence links General Mladic to any meeting when this crime was discussed -- when this JCE would have been entered into. Now having determines that this mystery meeting have to have happened, the Prosecution uses it to discount the words of General Mladic at the third Fontana meeting where he gives a choice to the Bosnian Muslims to stay or go. And the Prosecution says: No, that's false. "He clearly had no intention to allow any Muslims to stay." That's paragraph 1171 of their brief. In essence, the Prosecution uses this mysterious, unproved, uncorroborated meeting. Any time that General Mladic says something that is favourable, they say he must be lying because it was determined otherwise at this meeting. Any time the Prosecution presents two alternatives, the Prosecution is admitting reasonable doubt exists. Now, if we can go to the next slide. The words and deeds of General Mladic repeatedly reinforce that he had no criminal intent as to captured Bosnian Muslim POWs in Srebrenica before he departed for Belgrade. The evidence is also clear that General Mladic, personally had no contemporary knowledge of any of the crimes he is charged with. Rather, the consistent evidence of both Prosecution and Defence witnesses is that the accused gave legitimate and appropriate orders for treatment of detained members of the 28th Division. Multiple witnesses, both Prosecution and Defence, talked about how the accused foresaw their treatment as POWs and then their exchange with the other side. RM292 [Realtime transcript read in error "RM229"] described how the accused spoke to POWs at Nova Kasaba and said: "Prisoners do not need to be afraid because they would return to their houses and be exchanged." That's at transcript page 12659. RM292 further testified that the detainees applauded the accused. That's on transcript page 12662.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Notably, the witness did not identify any illegal orders of the accused as to the POWs. Another witness, Subotic, himself a military policeman, confirmed that at Nova Kasaba the accused told POWs that they would be exchanged and that they applauded him. That's at transcript page 32826-32827. Subotic further confirmed that the accused said the POWs would be transported to Bratunac, housed, fed, and transferred to civilian authorities for the taking of information and to be exchanged; that's in D926, paragraphs 29 through 30. Then the express orders of the accused to the military police present was to provide physical protection to the POWs and as described by Subotic: "And he told us, and told us strictly, to take care of the prisoners, that some buses would be arriving within an hour, that the men should sign their names, and that they would -- should all board the bus and deliver it to the civilian police in Bratunac. That is what I heard and I saw this when General Mladic was present there at the stadium." Transcript page 32826-32827. According to the evidence, Subotic followed these legitimate orders of the accused, providing water for detainees, and protecting the same until handing them over to the civilian police, D926, paragraph 31. Thus, we have evidence of express orders of the accused that run counter to the commission of any killings or crimes. There is also evidence that wounded persons present at this site were provided medical treatment and/or sent to the hospital, D926, paragraph 32 through 36. Such acts are consistent with the accused's words that these POWs would be treated properly and exchanged and are inconsistent with any plans to kill. RM0346 was a POW at Nova Kasaba and he too confirms what Subotic and RM292 stated about the express words of the accused. Specifically, RM0346 stated the accused said that they would go for lunch to Bratunac and would all later be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you referring to RM0346 or RM0364?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have written down here in my notes 346 but I see on the screen 364. I can clarify that by saying I'm referring to Exhibit P1118, page 9, and that should hopefully apply to only one witness unless we have bigger problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your team may be able to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Probably. It's RM0346. RM253, likewise, was at Nova Kasaba and he reiterated hearing the accused express: "You do you not have to worry. You will be exchanged and join your families in Tuzla. Now you will be transported by trucks to Bratunac or Kravica, where you will spend the night and get some food." And that is at T12532 and P1547, paragraph 20. Witness Jovic -- Jovicic, the driver for MUP commander Borovcanin, recalled the accused speaking to detainees of the 28th Division at Sandici meadows, at which time the accused also specified that: "Transport of their women and children towards Kladanj and Tuzla was in progress and that they would be transported." There is no credible evidence linking General Mladic's presence to any of the alleged killing or execution sites or evidencing his contact with any POWs, apart from that which we have just discussed. The above demonstrates the express orders of the accused that did not include any orders to kill. Momir Nikolic is the only witness who claimed to have a non-verbal hand gesture - just to be clear, he described it as thus: [Indicates] - from the accused from Nikolic interpreted that hand gesture as meaning that all would be killed. But the preposterous nature of his testimony and the dubious credibility of Nikolic are discussed in detail in our final brief. In fact, much of the Prosecution's evidence about orders given to VRS personnel allegedly from the accused as to the Srebrenica killings originate in one way or another from the dubious and discredited Nikolic. As such, it is a reasonable conclusion that Nikolic, in fact, was promoting a false notion. We cannot stress enough that despite Momir Nikolic's self-serving testimony about some sort of hand gesture, he testified that he never received a direct order from anyone - that includes Mladic - to commit the killings in Srebrenica which Nikolic went on to do. That's D1228, page 3. So again, Nikolic admits participating in killings, admits he never got an order to do so. The claim that a hand gesture like this one [Indicates] could be interpreted as an order to kill, is not even made by Momir Nikolic, but that doesn't stop this Prosecution from trying to use the same to invent a kill order that does not exist. Such a position is preposterous. Mladic could have been telling Nikolic: Go away and leave me alone. He could have been saying incredulously: Weren't you just listening to what I told them? He could have been saying: I have no time for your stupid question. Reasonable doubt exists. In any event, OTP investigator Bruce Bursik made clear that the Prosecution could not corroborate that the purported encounter of Momir Nikolic and Mladic at the roadside ever even happened. Nikolic's story of why he was there changes. In one version he was ordered there by Colonel Blagojevic. In the other, he was ordered there by his own subordinate within the military police. Neither makes sense. Plus, Mr. Bursik confirmed that Mladic never mentioned the infamous hand gesture except --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me start again. Mr. Bursik confirmed that Momir Nikolic never mentioned the purported hand gesture by Mladic, except for the first time in that one interview that the Prosecution decided not to record and that Momir Nikolic was generally evasive and not forthcoming. Your Honours, however you look at the evidence of Momir Nikolic, reasonable doubt creeps in. Thus, the Prosecution's evidence, when taken at its highest, demonstrates a set of facts where the explicit words of the accused directed towards the detained POWs of the 28th Division that they would be exchanged and reunited with their families, such words exclude the possibility that he intended to kill them or knew of any plans to kill them. Absent any explicit orders to the contrary, this evidence must be accepted as indicating the accused did not issue any orders nor intend the deaths of these individuals. Now, I want to just touch on some of the alleged murders. We have dealt with each in detail in our brief, but let's highlight Kravica because that is why I am flabbergasted and at a loss for words at what the Prosecution claims. Your Honours will recall that we heard evidence - and it was conceded by Mr. McCloskey the other day - that hours after Mladic had left the area and is en route to Belgrade, a bus of detainees was being transported by the MUP to Kravica warehouse. And some Bosnian Muslim detainees overpowered the guards, grabbed the weapons, and engaged in a fire-fight with the guards, killing one, and then one guard burned his hand taking back a gun and the revolt was thus stopped. We have no way of knowing how many detainees died in the fire-fight before that situation was ended. And then we know and agree that after this the MUP guards took revenge upon and killed countless detainees. The second set of killings can be nothing but a crime, but not one that was ordered by anyone. Now last week, I listened to Mr. McCloskey tell you and the public that: "It's the Prosecution case that this incident was an organised execution pursuant to orders, with the burned hands incident happening well after the executions had begun and it was a desperate response by a Muslim man to the executions around him, not how they started." That's at transcript page 44544. Then he started telling everyone how this conclusion was "obvious" from analysing the evidence. That's the next page, 44545. But no evidence has said that. If we go to the next page -- slide. Let's look at Erin Gallagher. Ms. Gallagher is Mr. McCloskey's investigator for Kravica and Srebrenica, and God bless her for telling the truth. She was an honest Prosecution member. And when first asked in cross-examination: "From your investigative work, have you gained knowledge about an incident where a group of detained Bosnian Muslim men tried to overpower the police guards that were guarding them, even talking the rifle of one guard and killing him and where another guard was injured trying to get that rifle back? Are you aware of such a instance? "A. I am aware of a instance at the Kravica warehouse where one Muslim man had grabbed the gun of -- it was -- had grabbed the gun and Rade Cutoric had wrestled the gun away and shortly after that the men on that side of the warehouse that were kept there were killed. "Q. And was it part of your investigation that prior to the incident where the individual tried to overpower and take the gun from this person, that no one had been shot at this location? "A. There was not a mass execution prior to this execution, not that I'm aware of no." Later on in re-direct, the Prosecution counsel Vanderpuye and Ms. Gallagher admitted that there's not concrete information either way, and we see the part of that transcript right there. So apparently what is obvious to Mr. McCloskey's colleagues, an investigator, is different than to him. Reasonable doubt exists when more than one possible conclusion exists. Now just to complete the picture, let's look at Mr. McCloskey' other investigator who spent considerable time investigating Kravica, Mr. Tomasz Blaszczyk. And at transcript page 12346 to 12347, he admitted that to him that it was still an open question which happened first. "A. Well, Your Honours, our investigation revealed that this incident with -- related to one guard who was killed by detainee, it happened. But when it happened, this is still open question for me, in fact, whether it happened because -- before that there was another killing take place and whether this incident, this particular incident, kind of sparked, you know, just the following events, it's just the killings of entire people, you know, which were kept in Kravica warehouse." Is it worrying that Prosecution counsel is molding the facts of their case to fit their theory, ignoring their own staff members who came as witnesses to give Your Honours evidence of these events? Case closed on Kravica. You must acquit. Now, as further indication of no prior intent for foul play, RM274 described that the Kravica guards were consistently kind toward the detainees in the beginning, referencing that cigarettes and water were provided. This is at P3098, page 24. RM274 estimates that this peaceful process continued 1.5 to 2 hours, P3098, page 19. No ill-treatment is alleged as to this time-period and RM274 reported that things only changed after an incident that made the guards angry when there was shooting outside. And RM274 likewise recalls a wounded guard was brought in, and only after that incident that the guards came in acting frightened and in a panic and started shooting detainees in the warehouse. There's also evidence suggesting that prior to arriving, MUP Commander Borovcanin had no idea what was going on and upon seeing the bodies at Kravica said: "Oh my God, what is this?" That's transcript page 33729 to 33721, the testimony of his driver, Nedjo Jovicic. Then Borovcanin went to go tell civilian municipal leaders what had happened. All of this, all of this leads to the reasonable conclusion of the lack of any plan to kill these persons and, rather, that an unfortunate act of revenge occurred when the attempted breakout occurred and when guards were killed and wounded. Mladic cannot be responsible for this under these facts. I want to just briefly turn on Trnovo. And the Prosecution admitted last week, talking about Trnovo: "And the Skorpions, I'm not going to show you that awful video but please take care here. Sometimes, because that video is so clear and the Muslims are so obviously from Srebrenica, we have not laid out the facts and the details of that crime as much as we should have. We have now. But this needs to be done to fully understand that this was part of the murder operation, part of the JCE to eliminate." Your Honours, pay attention to what Prosecution counsel just said. If they have conceded that they have not laid out the facts and details as they should have, they have not met their burden. Acquittal is warranted. I had not go through the other murder charges but urge you to heed that which we have analysed in our brief. We believe as to every such one, there remains serious doubts and ambiguities and even contradictions from the Prosecution's evidence, such that reasonable doubt has not been removed and an acquittal is appropriate. And we also ask you to take note of the evidence as to Mr. Mladic's horrified reaction after returning from Belgrade because that demonstrates that he certainly did not order the killing of anyone. The Defence has also set out in pages 869 to 873 of the final brief the post factum matters that affected his ability to do anything after the fact. Now I would like to return to the alibi, the time-period when General Mladic left Srebrenica and was in Belgrade. First off, the Prosecution has tried to point to Obradovic's generic testimony to indicate that Mladic would not relinquish command unless gone for more than seven days. Your Honours, why do they ignore the sworn testimony of their own witness, General Manojlo Milovanovic, who testified under oath and without any qualms or reservations and did not shirk from affirming that, when Mladic was gone - from the theatre or from the RS - he, General Milovanovic, assumed command and was in charge of the VRS. We see that at transcript page 11751 and 16950. And we also have to point out - if we can have the next slide - that the evidence is that rather than being involved in killings or killing sites, General Mladic is at a secret meeting in Dobanovci, Belgrade, 14 to 15 July 1995, meeting with these UN and European negotiators and Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic. As part of this meeting as D1413 [sic] evidences, General Mladic entered into agreement with General Smith to allow ICRC access to the POWs detained at Srebrenica. Now, common sense and logic dictate that from this agreement, we can conclude that General Mladic has no idea about any plans to kill the POWs of Srebrenica, because otherwise he would be stupid to enter into such agreement. The Defence submits that this evidence leads to the reasonable conclusion that General Mladic honestly believed that his orders to treat the detained members of the 28th Division as POWs until their release with the other side and that he had no idea that others were killing said persons. The document D1413 [sic] also identifies that Mladic wanted all generals of opposing sides to meet, to finally do a complete cessation of hostilities. This is consistent with his words to detainees before he left Bosnia, that soon they would be exchanged with the other side. General Mladic had his mind set on a permanent and lasting peace, not on revenge, nor atrocities. Why is the Prosecution ignoring the evidence of this meeting for which we have ample evidence while pushing their mysterious meeting of 11 July which is nowhere in the evidence? Because this meeting in Dobanovci establishes reasonable doubt. General Mladic's orders to the POWs never changed and that proves that he did not have the intent to kill them. This was done by others, including avengers, locals, and rogue members of the security organs. Now, just a few more points relating to Srebrenica. The bulk of the Prosecution case resolves around purported radio relay communication intercepts, which we have in detail analysed in our brief to demonstrate that pursuant to science, technology, and logic they could not be intercepted by the ABiH or other parties as alleged. I would only add to that that RM275 is someone that the Prosecution brought to authenticate some of these intercepts. However, their other witness, RM279, disavowed that RM275 could have been the drafter of the records in question. That's at transcript page 13557 to 13558. Both RM279 and official records of the ABiH demonstrate that RM275 wasn't even working in the interception unit during the time-period of the intercepts in question. He started working there in 1996. D316, D1463. Accordingly, this raises significant and reasonable doubt as to the authenticity of these intercepts. We have also gone into great detail about the forensic evidence of the mass graves in our final brief. I will not belabour those points, but we do want to highlight some key points. First, the evidence demonstrates that in some of these mass graves attributed to July 1995, human remains were found in ZOV body-bags. P1737, P1983, P1448, P1987. We heard from Dr. Stankovic that he created and used these bags for remains in 1992 and that the supply was used up after 1993, transcript page 43277-43278. That would raise significant reasonable doubt that bodies in the mass graves could be inclusive of persons who died in the years prior, whose remains were could mingled in the graves, and indeed that conclusion is consistent with evidence presented by Prosecution witnesses that Momir Nikolic, in fact, robbed graves from the years prior at the same time he robbed the Srebrenica graves. We can see that at transcript page 11485 to 11486. This set of facts thus calls into question the evidence of Srebrenica victims and calls for an acquittal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for bringing that to my attention. In the case we have been talking for a long time about combat casualties of the 28th Division being included as victims of execution by the Prosecution. During our proceedings, however, no fewer than four forensic professionals gave their expert opinions for what the Prosecution calls blindfolds, evidencing executions, that they could actually be bandanas worn by fighters that fell over they eyes as the body and particularly the ears decayed. The late Dr. Dunjic at D1448 and D1449; Dr. Stankovic, transcript page 43463; Dr. Chris Lawrence, transcript page 14802-14804; and Mr. Pecerelli at 18442 and 18443. Your Honour, Judge Orie, even said this was common knowledge, transcript page 14803 [Realtime transcript read in error "14083"]. The Prosecution has scoffed at such a suggestion, but the Prosecution's evidence indicates that ligatures and blindfolds found in Srebrenica mass graves, including loose in the grave, were sometimes pink or red in colour and brown with flowers. P1735, P1740. And now let's look here at some of the photographic evidence of ABiH fighters with bandanas and ribbons. We have the extracts from the videos that are in e-court as D339 and D340 respectfully, and here the last two on the slide are most instructive. These are actual images of actual ABiH fighters from the Srebrenica column when they arrived in Tuzla. And so, Your Honours, reasonable doubt is raised that some victims of execution are actually combat casualties buried with bandana and identifying ribbons, not blindfolds or ligatures. Your Honours, no matter where one picks to investigate more fully, the Srebrenica evidence falls apart as to General Mladic. The Prosecution is relying on you to fill in the blanks in the evidence with the story you would expect to hear. They did not do their job and major gaps remain. Reasonable doubt exists; therefore, the only appropriate and fair remedy is to enter an acquittal of General Mladic. I next move to Count 11, hostage taking. UN personnel actively participated in the war. There was thus a legitimate basis to detain. The Prosecution provided a flat narrative driven by criminal intent without the full picture. If we can have the first slide. Witness Dragicevic's statement described the legitimate detention of UN personnel: "Specific elements of UNPROFOR forces were actively involved in guiding the NATO aviation and rapid intervention forces towards Serbian targets. Removing them from their positions eliminated the possibility of them guiding the air force and artillery. This was, in essence, a protective and defence measures. It bears emphasising that the human shields allegation of hostage-taking is primarily only 10 to 20 detainees over one or two days. While UN detainees were held at Serb locations, the precise locations were never conveyed to deter anyone. Count 11 fails because of, one, a defective indictment; and two, the evidence fails to prove each element. Count 11 is defective for three reasons. First, the Prosecution imported the Common Article 3 language, non-international armed conflicts, to charge a situation involving internationalised conflict. We can go to the next slide. The Prosecution confused the determination that Common Article 3 may be applicable to non-international and international armed conflicts, as relieving the Prosecution of their duty to charge the correct language. That confusion is evident at transcript page 44323. How is charging the language alleging a non-international conflict proper in the situation of an internationalised armed conflict? No conviction against the accused can be entered when material facts are omitted. We get that from the Karadzic case, the decision on the accused's motion for relief for defects in the indictment, 30 September 2014, paragraph 15. How can a Chamber find an international armed conflict when it is not pleaded? Moreover, abandoning Common Article 3's exclusive application to non-international conflicts undermines customary law. Second, the Prosecution's failure to notify about material facts. While Common Article 3 may apply to international and non-international armed conflicts, this does not alleviate the Prosecution of pleading their case. Importing Common Article 3 failed to specify any internationalised chapeau, a material fact. The Prosecution has not cured this by providing "timely, clear, and consistent information detailing the factual basis," as was required in the Karadzic case on the same decision we mentioned, paragraph 15. Notice of "all IHL" is insufficient and prejudice the Defence. Third, if the character of the conflict is irrelevant as to Common Article 3 as Karadzic appeal decision implies, that's Karadzic decision on appeal of Trial Chamber's decision on preliminary motion to dismiss Count 11 of the indictment, 9 July 1992, paragraph 25, this improperly lowers the Prosecution burden. Alleviating proof of this element undermines a fair trial. It enables the Prosecution to more easily prove the alleged crime; and therefore, Count 11 is defective. Are we at the time for the break, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Should this Chamber find that Count 11 is not defective, Count 11 still fails on the merits as set out in section 6 of our final brief. First I will address self-defence and unjustified NATO bombings. Then I will address how Count 11 fails for four reasons: First, a legitimate basis to detain existed; second, improper treatment was perpetrated by paramilitaries; three, VRS ordered compliance with Geneva Conventions; and four, no reliable evidence proves a JCE. Contrary to the Prosecution's portrayal of justified NATO bombings, the NATO attacks that sparked prisoner of war detention sprung from an unfair situation, where the UN had previously agreed to allow weapons withdrawal from weapon collection points in self-defence and then went back on that agreement. If we can have the next slide. First, around 14 February 1994, the protocol between UNPROFOR and the VRS delineated that "the BSA reserves the right to implement adequate measures of self-defence." D112, page 4. GRM097 confirmed that weapons collection points were established around Sarajevo "so that if attacked ... they could then defend themselves." Transcript page 40119. Importantly, if attacked the party that was attacked therefore was no longer bound by the demilitarised aspect of that agreement, again 40119. The protocol in question demonstrates UN involved and uses the term "BSA" which is UN lingo. And appears on UNPROFOR Command fax letterhead. As of August 1994, BiH activity had already prompted the VRS to withdraw their weapons, D112, para 1 to 3. On 5 September 1994, UNPROFOR came off the original agreement, including the right to self-defence, saying that they "did not endorse this position." That's at P631, page 1. The Bosnian Muslim side was equally restricted but, around March 1994, the Serb side had already reported to UNPROFOR the repeated violations by the Muslim side; D111 is evidence of that. UNPROFOR did not conduct airstrikes against Muslim forces for violations because of American and NATO reluctance to act against the ABiH. We heard about that from GRM097, GRM037, General Rose, and Mr. Harland. In Witness Dragicevic's words, UNPROFOR had sided with the Muslims, D554, paragraph 31. Therefore, the Serb side withdrew weapons for self-defence. The UN ignored this legitimate purpose, bombing them instead. Turning to the legitimate basis to detain. Serb forces ultimately did not consider UNPROFOR to be neutral but rather combatants. GRM037 told us about that. It is necessary to show that the violation was committed against persons who were not directly involved in the hostilities. That's what the Blaskic Trial Judgement tells us at paragraph 177. Thus, the legitimate basis to detain UN combatants excludes UN POWs from Common Article 3. Equally important, this legitimate detention substantiates that the VRS detained personnel to prevent more bombings. Evidence substantiates a reasonable alternative, that UN personnel were detained as combatants as they were exchanging gun-fire, P591; holding territory, D554; enlisting NATO air-strikes, P2558; guiding pilots to Serb targets, P6644; collecting intelligence against, Serbs transcript 39023; smuggling weapons to the enemy forces against the VRS, D535; and even taking VRS soldiers prisoner, D1586, P2558. Around 27 May 1995, RM401 testified about the UN's armed re-taking of a bridge assisted by ABiH "support fire." Example, that means the ABiH was shooting to cover and assist UN personnel; that's at transcript page 18260. This substantiates that VRS could have reasonably perceived the UN and the ABiH as co-operating, that the UN were combatants. Around 28 May 1995, in reaction to how the UN had taken detained Serb soldiers, this memo declared that: "UN has not the legal right to hold prisoners of war." It describes that: "The credibility of UN regarding international humanitarian law is also deranged if such a practice is being implemented." Again, that's D1586. Not one occasion occurred where UNPROFOR requested and launched NATO to bomb the Bosnian Muslim side. On the other hand, UN personnel recorded the VRS locations and some trained as airplane spotters acted in that role. For targeting, UN ground personnel communicated to the NATO pilot directly; General Smith told us about that. During the testimony of UNPROFOR General Nicolai, Judge Orie asked: "Had UNPROFOR provided assistance to NATO to define those targets on Bosnian Serb territory? " The response was: "Yes. The targets were determined at UNPROFOR headquarters in Sarajevo, and that information was subsequently relaid to NATO with a request to fire there." UNPROFOR endorsed the large-scale NATO air-strikes of May 1995, D1468, page 9. The Bosnian Serb leadership considered that the UN had become combatants. General Smiths' now declassified correspondence to the US -- not to his UN superiors, but to the US, reports on 27 May 1995 that "I've broken the machine." That's D1462. On 28 May 1995, another declassified cable details Smith advocating that the only options are to become unsustainably weak or to wage was, D452. In his ICTY statement, General Smith conceded: "We were never peacekeepers ... because there was no peace to keep" and "we were bombing one party." Segers also reported a Pakistani UNPROFOR colonel taking a Bosnian Muslim side when an UNMO reported that the Bosnian Muslims were shelling their own village, to blame the Serb. This colonel responded: "You are liars," D1465, page 11. Improper treatment was perpetrated by paramilitaries as in our final brief, paragraph 3349 to 3386. Importantly, VRS officer Vojvodic was tasked by General Tolimir with taking over and securing UN detainees. Vojvodic took over as the primary guard and no one was maltreated, D1224, paragraph 9. The Red Cross visited them in June 1995 without complaints, D1227. As to the bridge, RM401 first described captors as Bosnian Serb forces but clarified that the majority were militia men, P2537. This meant: "People who take up arms, who put uniforms that they find on the ground and they operate with or without uniforms and they take part in fighting next to the regular army." That's what RM401 said at 18238 to 18239. RM401 was reassured of being handed over to the Serbian regular army, P2537. Once in VRS custody, detainees were treated according to the Geneva Conventions which were read aloud, transcript page 18263, again RM401. VRS orders substantiate the intent of the VRS to treat UN personnel as POWs, including IHL brochures. One VRS order on 27 May 1995 states: "Make sure that UNPROFOR are treated properly as prisoners of war," P789, paragraph 4. Colonel Sehovac detained POWs, stressing that: "We did not mistreat them ... we abided by the Geneva Conventions." Transcript page 24052. Around 26 May 1995, as the French contingent had received orders not to surrender, the VRS and French agreed for the VRS to shoot outside and for the French to then surrender, P6717 and transcript page 25215 to 25217. From this, it is clear that UN personnel and the VRS co-operated to peacefully resolve the issues. No one was ever endangered. Evidence substantiates proper POW treatment. Witness Cornish testified that detainees used the radio to report back hourly. He also said that they were allowed to wash their clothes. Witness Vojvodic confirmed that the detainees, the POWs, wrote letters and received the Red Cross. Several witnesses, including General Riley and Colonels Radojcic and Sehovac even testified that UN personnel held as POWs were even permitted to keep their weapons. No reliable evidence provides a plan or agreement involving the accused, literally nothing. In an alleged intercept from 28 May 1995 between General Smith and General Mladic, that's P790, Mladic claimed the hostages were held by the VRS but only to posture. First, paramilitaries committed the impermissible acts against a few UN personnel; secondly, General Mladic learned about this like everyone else on the TV; third, General Mladic orders his troops via General Tolimir and via Mr. Vojvodic to take over and detain these persons as POWs; and then, fourth, General Mladic speaks to Smith, tacitly taking responsibility for bad acts to try to gain an upper hand; fifth, the General's bluff does not work but no more POWs are put at the radio antennas or in harm's way after he has this discussion with General Smith. So there are no acts that could be tied to a criminal nature from the words that General Mladic uttered in this conversation. Therefore, Count 11 fails because the indictment is defective and even based on the evidence it cannot be said that the only conclusion is that the VRS under Mladic's orders took UN personnel as hostages in order to deter NATO strikes. Instead, the evidence demonstrates legitimate detention of combatant POWs. They were treated in accord with the Geneva Conventions. No conviction can be arise for Count 11. I will now move to the topic of mitigation and sentencing submissions. I hope that we have been abundantly clear in our final brief, particularly section VII of the same, pages 899 onward; as well as in the past days in our oral submissions, that we believe the only fair and just outcome is an acquittal, due to the fact that the Prosecution has failed to meet its burden of proof as to General Ratko Mladic. However, as Your Honours know but the public may not know, we are required by the particular Rules of the Tribunal to make these submissions now. I had not repeat too much submissions already made in our brief. The Prosecution's comments the other day are inappropriate. Everybody deserves mitigation if it exists under the evidence, especially General Mladic. ICTY jurisprudence states that expressions of remorse can be recognised as a mitigating factor if the remorse is real and sincere. Indeed prior ICTY cases like the Oric trial judgement have considered remorse even where the accused made no statement but where throughout the trial the counsel expressed it on his behalf, that's at paragraph 752. In the instant case, counsel have repeatedly made expressions on behalf of and at the instruction of the accused. Some illustrative examples include in relation to witnesses RM084, RM079, RM010, RM115, and RM291. There is likewise evidence of Mladic's own statements that demonstrate remorse. We highlight one such instances introduced by the Prosecution through Commander Rupert Smith. Mladic is recorded in relation to Markale to have said: "Our side does not have any high-impact projectiles of this kind, one of which could hurt so many people, and I'm very sorry, er for the misfortune which befell all these people, be they killed or wounded." That's P789. Another instance is the evidence that indicates he only found out about some killings having taken place in Srebrenica after the fact and was visibly upset upon learning of the same. Witness Simic talked about that at transcript page 32589. After finding out, Mladic was visibly distraught and worried and condemned the acts as being horrible. Witness Todic talked about that, D798, paragraph 28. He further stated that whoever is responsible for those acts must be crazy. The same citation, D798, paragraph 28. If the Prosecution promotes the notebooks of the accused as authentic, then they must also accept that these purport to show the accused advocating a commission to be formed on the basis of equal parity. To really investigate all the deaths and killings around Srebrenica, P348, page 47. Next I move to the sentencing provisions of the SFRY, which prohibit any sentence exceeding 15 years or 20 years for the most atrocious crimes. Although this Tribunal has decried that it is not bound by the SFRY sentencing practices, this Tribunal is bound by international law, i.e., it must apply the law that was in force at the time of the commission of the crimes nullen crimen sine lege, nullum poena sine lege. Consequently, any sentence that would exceed the parameters of the 1976 Criminal Code of the SFRY would be a violation of the principle of legality and of the prohibition of the retroactive application of the law. Similarly, the European Court of Human Rights has recently affirmed this same rule as to Bosnia-Herzegovina; it should apply to this Tribunal as well. The law in force at the time of the commission of the crimes alleged was the 1976 Criminal Code which remained authoritative until 1998 in the BiH and 2000 in the Republika Srpska. It dictates that war crimes are to be punished by imprisonment that falls within five to 15 years or by the death penalty for the most serious crimes. Nevertheless, the death penalty was abolished by the Dayton Agreement and substituted by the possibility to impose a 20-year term. The prohibition on retroactivity inherently implies a prohibition on the retroactive application of lex gravior, i.e., of the most -- of the more severe penalty. Consequently, it is unlawful to impose a heavier penalty which did not exist at the material time of the commission of the crimes. It is a widely recognised principle of international law that whenever a crime is punishable under two successive provisions, one of them being more lenient, the lesser should be applied as per the favor libertatis principle. I refer you to the Maktouf and Damjanovic versus BiH decision of the European Court of Human Rights, page 11. Likewise, from that same decision, paragraph -- page 46, the prohibition on retroactivity is part of customary international law and a preemptory norm of international law, therefore permitting no derogations. In dealing with the very same issue, the European Court of Human Rights deemed the application of the 2003 BiH Criminal Code instead of the 1976 SFRY code to be unlawful and a breach of the applicants' rights, page 32 of the Maktouf-Damjanovic decision. In sum, the application by the Chamber of a penalty not envisioned under the applicable law at the time would be a violation of the customary international law norm prohibiting the retroactive application of the law. Consequently, the Chamber is under an obligation to ensure that the penalty falls within the five to 15 years parameters or 20 years for the most serious crimes that would otherwise have been punished by the death penalty. Not doing so would mean that the Tribunal is acting ultra vires. What message would this Tribunal be sending the world if it persisted in sentencing practices that the European Court of Human Rights has now forbidden, forbidden domestic jurisdictions from pursuing as unjust? We submit that the very legacy and reputation of the ICTY is called into question if it opposes and acts in violation of the standard proclaimed by the European Court of Human Rights. I now turn to Prosecution's assertions as to aggravating circumstances. The Prosecution has failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt an abuse of the accused's position of authority. In any event, a high-ranking position of authority does not, per se, deserve a more severe sentence; and in any event, the accused did not abuse his position of authority in any manner whatsoever. The Prosecution repeatedly emphasised that there was a clear hierarchy within the VRS within which orders had to be respected. Nevertheless, this clear hierarchy is irrelevant in respect to the accused's liability, since no order that could connect him to the crimes has been put forth by the Prosecution. Again, as to Srebrenica, Prosecution excerpt Richard Butler stated that he had not come across any orders from the accused ordering the commission of the crimes. It is therefore unreasonable to say in light of the evidence that the accused abused his authority for criminal purposes. In any event, this Chamber should reject this ground as an aggravating factor because it has not been raised by the Prosecution in the indictment and, as such, it is not meeting the conditions for aggravating factors. The Prosecution has argued the special vulnerability of victims as aggravating. Such an approach is not allowed to be taken into account twice due to the prohibition of double counting, insofar as it has already been subsumed in the overall gravity of the crimes. Look to the Kordic and Cerkez appeals judgement, paragraph 1089; and the Stakic appeals judgement, paragraph 413; and the Galic appeals judgement, paragraph 408. In its submissions at paragraph 1743 of their final brief, the Prosecution can only put forward anecdotal evidence which bears no legal significant and has failed to bring forth any appropriate expert reports or studies. The Prosecution likewise maintains that the accused should get the maximum sentence solely because he should get a higher sentence than subordinates. This is completely at odds with and in compatible with the principle of individualisation of the penalty and legal certainty. Such a position by the Prosecution represents a conviction by extension through collective guilt. Again, it goes back to the desire to pump of Ratko Mladic to superhuman proportions to make him the symbolic sacrificial lamb for the perceived guilt of all Serbs as perceived and assessed by the Prosecution. Another Prosecution claim made at paragraph 1741 of their final brief is that the accused took a dominant role in the commission of the crimes by not respecting IHL; but this is directly refuted by the many orders in evidence from the accused commanding the exact opposite. Further, the Prosecution claim at paragraph 1737 of their final brief that Mladic's subordinates summarily executed thousands in Srebrenica, but this is irrelevant absent the required nexus. It is also impermissible double counting, in that this is the subsumed in the crime alleged. Now I would ask that we move in private session.

utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From Mr. Darko Mladic's statement, we see that the accused raised him with a spirit of helping everyone regardless of ethnicity. The most important thing was to be a good human being, paragraph 8, and Mr. Darko Mladic details various good deeds performed by his father to assist non-Serb civilians, both during the war and outside of the war. We consider that to be evidence in mitigation. In summation, we ask you to reject the Prosecution's efforts to apply collective guilt, to build up Mr. Mladic to superhuman proportions, and their call for you to act contrary to various legal maxims in imposing a life sentence. The appropriate standard and legal principles dictate that any sentence should be limited and minimum in nature, due to the mitigating and other circumstances enumerated. Your Honours, for all the reasons stated these past three days, the Defence would submit that the Prosecution has failed to meet the requisite burden of proof as to any of the counts and charges in the indictment. It simply did not present the evidence necessary to prove its case and support the allegations it made in the indictment. We thus feel that only just verdict would be acquittal. Now I would like to take a few moments to address some additional words. Your Honours, today my client speaks through me as his attorney, and it is his words whose burden that I now turn to to speak to you. It is a heavy burden to speak for a man who has been so completely and deliberately misunderstood, who has had to listen to vicious allegations against himself day after day. It is a difficult position that not many of us could endure quietly. At times, his emotions have gotten to him, and, and as you know from the medical reports, his medical condition is such that it is not his fault, it is a medical condition that contributes to emotional outbursts. With this Tribunal unable to accommodate his medical condition, do not hold it against my client that you expelled him from court in the past. But more importantly, try to see things from his perspective. And to prepare for today, I tasked myself with the same task, and to do so, I looked at what my client said in the Karadzic proceedings on 28 May 2014 when he was summoned by the power of subpoena to essentially be forced to potentially be a witness against his own interests in a case under the same indictment. Therein he stated, and now I quote from that transcript: "THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, ladies and gentlemen, as for this Hague Tribunal, this Court, I cannot stand it, and I do not recognise it, and I cannot testify before it. I cannot take an oath because this is pressure against me as a person, against my health, against my people. These continue to be sanctions, and things have really been brought do an end. "I kindly request that you give me the following possibility. With all due respect to President Radovan Karadzic and the efforts that he made and has made for the salvation of our people, and I contributed somewhat to doing some good, I wouldn't want this trial to fail, so I would like to ask you, if you have the possibility and the time, to hear me out. I wrote seven pages last night before Saint Sava's Day. Today is Saint Sava's Day. So if you don't mind, I would like to read that out. And after that, I can take an oath. "I do not recognise this Hague Court. It is a NATO creation. It is a Satanic court, not a court of justice, and it is trying us because we are Serbs, because we protect our people from you." And then Judge Kwon said: "Mr. Mladic, I am cutting you off. Please be seated. I will consult my colleagues." Mr. Kwon then said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... did you say "The Hague court" or "the hate court."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The Hague court, with a G.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "Judge Kwon: Mr. Mladic, as you know, we have our rules in which our proceedings should proceed. So I would recommend you, again, to take the oath ... answer the question, if you will ..." and the questions posed Mr. Karadzic. And then there was a discussion again as to the rules of the procedure and then my client finally said: "THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, you are considerably younger than I am. You are exerting pressure against me for no reason whatsoever. I'm not afraid of anyone but God. My conscience is clear with regard to all matters. "Your subpoenas and your platitudes at The Hague Tribunal and your false indictments, I don't care one bit about any of that. I don't want to tire these people over there, and all of you. I am going to make this statement but I do not recognise your court, The Hague Tribunal. It does not exist for me." Now, that is what my client said, and I can tell you that he believed every word the day that he uttered them. For him, that was the truth. And I have to ask you: Can we really blame him if his view of this Tribunal is so negative if it is based on how he has felt -- based upon how he feels he has been treated since coming here? I want you to appreciate where he is coming from and in rendering your verdict and judgement to try your best to prove him wrong, because I have been unable to come up with arguments to convince him otherwise, though I have tried. And can you really blame my client for having such a negative view? If we can have the next slide. This is the motto that hangs in the lobby of the Tribunal and it shows no respect nor acknowledgement for the presumption of innocence nor the protection of the rights of the accused. It just says: "Bringing war criminals to justice and justice to victims." Can you really blame my client for having a negative view, given that you ejected him at the time of the Initial Appearance from merely trying to invoke his right to waive reading of the indictment, a right all my prior clients enjoyed and exercised. Instead, you kicked him out and read the indictment anyway. And the next accused who was arrested, Mr. Hadzic, he simply asked the Court not to read the indictment and this was complied with. Can you really blame my client from being leary of the fact that two out of the three Judges have made affirmative findings of guilt against him? You, Judge Orie in the Galic case; and you, Judge Fluegge, in Tolimir. Can you blame him for being skeptical about these proceedings and his rights being protected given that both the president of the MICT who made a public statement to the victims of Srebrenica that Karadzic and Mladic will be brought to justice and the ICTY president who made affirmative findings of guilt in the Popovic case against him? Can you really blame my client for being afraid of injustice, given that the Karadzic case also made affirmative findings of guilt in the Judgement against him? And then Your Honours brought over the helpers from that case to draft this Judgement, which you have recently acknowledged might already be in the process of being written. Can you really blame my client when the Appeals Chamber has already in the Popovic appeal again made multiple findings of guilt against him in another case where he could not defend himself? Can you blame him in this case where the Prosecution was allowed to eavesdrop on his communications with counsel and thus break the attorney/client privilege? Your Honours, you have to understand and appreciate why my client does not trust you. And now your job is to look at all the evidence, and I hope that you will do so and take the opportunity to do what I cannot do, which is to convince my client that this Tribunal is fair and is just and that you will fairly appraise the evidence and not bow to Prosecution arguments or political pressure, and you will make sure that the highest standard of the burden of proof pyramid is applied. I hope that you do, and I hope that you prove my client wrong, and in doing so hopefully you will enlighten those of them -- those persons out there in the public, out there, who might feel the same way my client does. An acquittal would prove my client wrong and would send a strong and enduring message as to the legacy of this Tribunal as one of justice. And I for one sincerely hope you choose that path. Lastly, we heard Mr. McCloskey read a poem or letter from the American Civil War last week. I don't have anything like that and, in any event, I'm not sure if that is relevant to our proceedings. General Mladic has asked me to leave you with something more relevant and meaningful. We have been speaking over the last four years about very specific issues and incidents, and it is very easy in a case like this to lose sight of the bigger picture. War is ugly. And in the end, its violence does not discriminate. General Mladic is a military man, but he watched his country descend into chaos and tear itself apart. It has shaken him profoundly and in ways that this Court can never begin to understand. He therefore has just one request. He would ask that we take one minute of silence to remember and commemorate all the victims of the senseless war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a war that I might add he neither started nor prolonged. And when I say "all victims," General Mladic wishes me to specify that he and the Defence team considers every life lost in the war, every Bosniak, Serb, Croat, Roma, Albanian, every man, woman and child a tragedy, and this list of victims includes the 1300 Serbs of the Srebrenica area who lost their lives to Naser Oric 's horrific violence and whose voice has not often been heard in this place. May their memory be eternal and may mankind have learned from their lessons because today we sorely need them. And that is all that General Mladic wished me to leave you with. So I leave it in your hands, Your Honours, if we will have the moment of silence or not. I have no further submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. The request you passed on from Mr. Mladic is denied. It doesn't fall within the scope of our task. And we will adjourn for the day. We will resume on Thursday, the 15th of December. And could I hear from the parties whether you have reached agreement to have it two times one and a half hour, or whether it would be three sessions, split up the middle session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From the Defence side, we have no problem with the proposed one and a half hour, then a break, and then one and a half hour sitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We didn't propose anything, but if that's what the parties prefer and if you have no problems, then we will head for two sessions of one and a half hour. Therefore, we'll adjourn for the day and we'll resume on Thursday, the 15th of December, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of December, 2016, at 9.30 a.m.
